Arioch
är'i-ok
n. (the captain of Nebuchadnezzar's guard charged with slaying the wise men of Babylon, who brought Daniel before the king; also a king of Ellasar in the confederacy of Chedorlaomer)
From Hebrew and Aramaic Aryok, probably from a root meaning lion-like, and by some traced to an Elamite or Hurrian original. Two men of the name stand a thousand years apart in the record, and Scripture keeps them distinct by their offices rather than their spelling.

Biblical Definition

Arioch is the officer through whom the whole crisis of Daniel 2 is turned. Nebuchadnezzar, tormented by a dream his magicians could neither recall nor read, “was angry and very furious, and commanded to destroy all the wise men of Babylon” (Dan 2:12), and the sentence swept up four Hebrew captives who had never been consulted: “they sought Daniel and his fellows to be slain” (Dan 2:13). Into that came the executioner. “Then Daniel answered with counsel and wisdom to Arioch the captain of the king&#39;s guard, which was gone forth to slay the wise men of Babylon” (Dan 2:14). The Authorized Version's counsel and wisdom renders a phrase meaning prudence and discretion; Daniel did not resist and did not plead, but asked a question — “Why is the decree so hasty from the king?” — and the captain answered him. Arioch then does two more things: he grants the delay, and when Daniel returns with the secret he takes him to the throne room himself, “in haste” (Dan 2:25), with a courtier's eagerness to be the man who found the solution. He is a pagan soldier doing his duty, and God used his willingness to stop and listen to spare the lives of every wise man in Babylon. The older Arioch is king of Ellasar in the four-king alliance that carried Lot away out of Sodom (Gen 14:1).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Arioch; in sacred history he is captain of the guard to Nebuchadnezzar, and also a king of Ellasar in the days of Abram.

ARIOCH, n. Lion-like; a proper name in the Hebrew Scriptures.

The captain of the king's guard under Nebuchadnezzar, charged to destroy the wise men.

To him Daniel answered with counsel and wisdom, and obtained a delay.

He brought Daniel in haste before the king to declare the interpretation.

Also, Arioch king of Ellasar, one of the four kings who warred against the cities of the plain.

Key Scripture

Dan 2:14 — "Then Daniel answered with counsel and wisdom to Arioch the captain of the king's guard, which was gone forth to slay the wise men of Babylon:"

Dan 2:15 — "He answered and said to Arioch the king's captain, Why is the decree so hasty from the king? Then Arioch made the thing known to Daniel."

Dan 2:24 — "Therefore Daniel went in unto Arioch, whom the king had ordained to destroy the wise men of Babylon: he went and said thus unto him; Destroy not the wise men of Babylon: bring me in before the king, and I will shew unto the king the interpretation."

Gen 14:1 — "And it came to pass in the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of nations;"

Modern Corruption

There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is the wisdom of the believer under an unjust decree: not defiance and not despair, but a discreet question and a request for time in which God may answer.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Arioch is a Babylonian officer and nobody has contested him. What the encounter sets against the modern instinct is Daniel's manner. A death squad is at the door on the authority of a tyrant's bad night, and the young man neither denounces the king nor bribes the captain nor flees. He answers with prudence, asks why, and requests an interval. The interval he uses for prayer: he goes to his three companions that they might desire mercies of the God of heaven concerning this secret.

The principle to recover is that faith under pressure is usually quiet and always dependent. Scripture praises “A soft answer turneth away wrath” (Pro 15:1), and Christ sent out His own with the same doubleness: “be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves” (Mat 10:16). Daniel's courage in chapter 6 is celebrated because he would not stop praying; his wisdom in chapter 2 is that he knew when to ask a captain a civil question. Both are obedience, and the church that can only manage the loud kind will lose men it might have kept.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Aryok (H746), Arioch; rab-tabbachiyn (H7227 with H2877), chief of the executioners, captain of the guard; Aramaic 'eta' (H5843), counsel; te'em (H2942), discretion, judgment; raz (H7328), secret, mystery.

expand to see more

Hebrew Aryok (H746) — Arioch; the captain of the guard and the king of Ellasar.

Hebrew tabbach (H2877) — executioner, guardsman; his office was literally chief slaughterer.

Aramaic 'eta' (H5843) — counsel; the first half of Daniel's answer.

Aramaic te'em (H2942) — taste, discretion, decree; the second half, and the king's decree also.

Aramaic raz (H7328) — secret; the word for the dream God revealed.

Usage

"“Arioch the captain of the king's guard” — the man sent to kill, met with a question."

"“Why is the decree so hasty from the king?” — prudence buying an hour for prayer."

"“Then Arioch brought in Daniel before the king in haste” — the courtier at his most useful."
